clinicalPearls: The presence of blood in the ejaculate, which is alarming to patients but is most often benign, particularly in younger men
In men under about 40 with no risk factors, an isolated or short-lived episode is usually self-limiting and needs only reassurance after a basic assessment
Persistent, recurrent, or high-volume haematospermia, and any case in men over 40, warrants fuller evaluation to exclude significant pathology
Common benign causes include inflammation or infection of the prostate, seminal vesicles, or ejaculatory ducts, and recent prostate biopsy or instrumentation
Important causes to exclude include prostate cancer, other genitourinary malignancy, tuberculosis or sexually transmitted infection, bleeding disorders, and, uncommonly, systemic hypertension
Assessment includes examination with digital rectal examination and blood-pressure measurement, urinalysis and culture, sexually transmitted infection screening, and PSA in the appropriate age group
Treatment is directed at any underlying cause, and where none is found reassurance and observation are appropriate, as most cases resolve spontaneously
reference.pathophysiology: Semen is derived largely from the seminal vesicles and prostate, and blood can enter it anywhere along the ejaculatory tract, including the prostate, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory ducts, vasa, and posterior urethra. The commonest mechanism is inflammation or infection producing fragile, congested mucosa that bleeds, or iatrogenic trauma after prostate biopsy or instrumentation. Obstruction and dilatation of the ejaculatory ducts, calculi, cysts, vascular malformations, and neoplasia are less frequent sources, while systemic factors such as coagulopathy or severe hypertension occasionally contribute. The age-related shift in likely aetiology explains why older men merit more thorough evaluation for malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Sexually transmitted infection or genitourinary tuberculosis
Ejaculatory duct obstruction, cyst, or calculi
additionalInvestigations: Sexually transmitted infection screen, including nucleic acid amplification testing
Digital rectal examination and blood-pressure measurement
PSA in men over 40 or with risk factors
MRI of the prostate and seminal vesicles
Transrectal ultrasound, with semen analysis and a coagulation screen where indicated
redFlags: Age over 40 with persistent or recurrent haematospermia
An abnormal prostate on examination or a raised PSA
Systemic features such as weight loss, fever, or night sweats suggesting tuberculosis or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Excellent in the great majority, particularly in younger men in whom episodes are self-limiting; the prognosis then depends on any identified underlying cause, most of which are treatable.
pitfalls: Over-investigating young men with a single self-limiting episode and no risk factors
Under-investigating men over 40 or those with persistent symptoms, missing prostate cancer or other serious pathology
Forgetting to check blood pressure and to take a coagulation and medication history
Overlooking recent instrumentation or prostate biopsy as an obvious benign cause
Not screening for infection, sexually transmitted infection, or tuberculosis where epidemiologically relevant
